messages.author: 809c86ffe9d447f3
messages.subject: Standardised coefficients being equal to standardised ones
parts:
The Beaujean textbook on lavaan and sem [1] says (in page 27)  that path coefficients are standardised by multiplying them by: (standard deviation of the predictor variable (X)/ std of outcome variable (X)). 

[1] Beaujean, A. A. (2014). Latent variable modeling using R: A step-by-step guide. Routledge.

In an example from the book, as seen below,  the standardised solutions (shown in the table at the bottom) are the same the unstandardised ones. This is the same case with my data. 

Why are standardised vs unstandardised variables the same in certain path models?
Does this have to do with having had standardised all my data (by passing it by the "scale" function in R) before fitting the model?




Thanks!

Can the z-value of an indirect effect be considered the effect size of that effect?

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Standardised coefficients being equal to standardised ones
parts: Aren't the z-values provided automatically by the lavaan output a standardised solution as well?
That "standardizes" the estimate by its SE, not the SDs of the predictor and outcome.
Why do we report lavaan's "standardized" solutions, such as the ones in the std.all column as opposed to the z-values?
As an effect size, like reporting standardized slopes for a regression model.
Can the z-value of an indirect effect be considered the effect size of that effect?
No, it is a (Wald z) test statistic, influenced by N, as opposed to a standardized effect size (independent of N).
the standardised solutions (shown in the table at the bottom) are the same the unstandardised ones. This is the same case with my data.
...
Does this have to do with having had standardised all my data (by passing it by the "scale" function in R) before fitting the model?

Yes, if your SDs are already 1, then the solution is already in units of SD.

FYI, you cannot trust your p values when you do that.  You can obtain p values for the standardized estimates from standardizedSolution().

Terrence D. Jorgensen

messages.author: bc810b1d0900407f
messages.subject: Re: Standardised coefficients being equal to standardised ones
parts:
Merely for illustration, I created a two-variable dataset and fitted a one-IV regression model to illustrate cases in which the SEs and CIs for a standardized regression coefficient based on these two approaches: raw data and than standardizedSolution(), the recommended way, and standardize variables first and use parameterEstimates(), the way not recommended, can be quite different.

# Standardized solution
set.seed(870431)
n <- 100
x <- rnorm(n)
b <- .7
y <- b * x + rnorm(n, 0, sqrt(1 - b^2))
dat <- data.frame(x = 5 * x, y = 4 * y)

mod <- "y ~ x"

library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-12
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.
# Original data
fit1 <- sem(mod, dat)
# Standardized data
fit2 <- sem(mod, data.frame(scale(dat)))

# Standardized coefficient: Raw data
print(standardizedSolution(fit1)[1, ], nd = 5)
#>   lhs op rhs est.std      se        z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
#> 1   y  ~   x 0.68408 0.04656 14.69117      0  0.59282  0.77535
# Standardized coefficient: Standardize variables first
print(parameterEstimates(fit2)[1, ], nd = 5)
#>   lhs op rhs     est      se       z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
#> 1   y  ~   x 0.68408 0.07294 9.37869      0  0.54112  0.82704

Not shown above but x is treated as fixed by default.

In this example, the standardized coefficient is a function of the estimates of the unstandardized coefficient, the variance of y, and the variance of x:

beta = b * sqrt(variance_x / variance_y)

However, the variance of y is not a free parameter in the model, but a function of the estimates of b, the variance of x, and the variance of the error term of y (displayed as "y ~~ y" in the parameter estimate table).

So, the sampling variance of beta, the standardized regression coefficient, is a function of the sampling variance and covariance of the estimates of b, the variance of x, and the variance of the error term. Even if x is treated as fixed and so it is not an estimate, the estimate of the variance of the error term is not fixed.

Moreover, there are cases in which we would like to treat x variables as random (setting fixed.x = FALSE). In these cases, then sampling variance of estimate of the variance of x (and its covariance with other estimates involved), will affect the SE of the standardized regression coefficient:

# Original data
fit1b <- sem(mod, dat, fixed.x = FALSE)
# Standardized coefficient: Raw data, fixed.x = FALSE
print(standardizedSolution(fit1b)[1, ], nd = 5)
#>   lhs op rhs est.std     se        z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
#> 1   y  ~   x 0.68408 0.0532 12.85804      0  0.57981  0.78836

The following example illustrate how to compute the standardized coefficient using ":=", and the SE, p-value, and CI are identical to those from standardizedSolution() (fixed.x = FALSE):

mod3 <-
"
y ~ b * x
y ~~ evar * y
x ~~ xvar * x
ysd := sqrt((b^2) * xvar + evar)
xsd := sqrt(xvar)
# Self-computed standardized
bstd := b * xsd / ysd
"

library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-12
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.

# Original data
fit3 <- sem(mod3, dat)
print(parameterEstimates(fit3), nd = 5)
#>    lhs op                   rhs label      est      se        z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
#> 1    y  ~                     x     b  0.54183 0.05777  9.37869      0  0.42860  0.65507
#> 2    y ~~                     y  evar  9.81441 1.38797  7.07107      0  7.09404 12.53478
#> 3    x ~~                     x  xvar 29.40457 4.15843  7.07107      0 21.25419 37.55495
#> 4  ysd := sqrt((b^2)*xvar+evar)   ysd  4.29501 0.30370 14.14214      0  3.69977  4.89026
#> 5  xsd :=            sqrt(xvar)   xsd  5.42260 0.38344 14.14214      0  4.67108  6.17412
#> 6 bstd :=             b*xsd/ysd  bstd  0.68408 0.05320 12.85804      0  0.57981  0.78836

In short, we should use standardizedSolution() because it takes into account the sampling variability of the standardizers (the SDs). If we standardize the variables first, their sampling variability, if any, is ignored.

I hope I understood how lavaan works on this regard. Please correct me if I am wrong.

-- Shu Fai

A side issue: For both standardizedSolution() and parameters defined by ":=", standard errors are derived by the delta method:

https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/i4OF4O0_Uv8/m/ZvkjkTPuAAAJ

Actually, in the one-IV-one-DV simple regression model above, you may recall the beta is equal to the Pearson's r between x and y. We know that the sampling distribution of Pearson's r is asymmetric (unless the population correlation is zero) and so usually we form asymmetric CI fora Pearson's r using methods such as Fisher's z transformation.

cor.test(dat$x, dat$y)
#> 95 percent confidence interval:
#>  0.5633636 0.7762064
#> sample estimates:
#>       cor
#> 0.6840844

Delta method yields symmetric CI. Nevertheless, in this example, the Fisher's z CI, [.536, .776] and delta method CI, [.580, .788], are not too different except for the lower limit.

messages.subject: Re: Standardised coefficients being equal to standardised ones
parts:
Oh ... while thinking about a reference to cite (sorry, I do not yet have one in my mind), I think there is a much much simpler explanation to say why standardizing all variables first to get the standardized solution can be wrong (my explanation is not entirely wrong, I believe, but I were thinking more from the perspective of regression than from SEM).

Let us consider the simple case in which we standardize all variables and then do SEM.

Recall that when we used the default settings in most SEM programs, we analyze covariance matrices (and mean vectors, if means are modeled). It uses the estimated sampling variances and covariances of all elements in the matrices, including the diagonals (the variances) to compute the SEs of parameters.

If we standardize all variables, the "covariance matrix" becomes a correlation matrix. The diagonal elements are necessarily equal to one regardless of data. No sampling variances for them. (The sampling variance of off-diagonal elements are also affected but it is sufficient to focus on the diagonal elements here.)

However, if we use this matrix as if it were a covariance matrix, then an SEM program will incorrectly treat the 1s as sample estimates with sampling variances, resulting in incorrect SEs.

In sum, for the case in which all variables are standardized first and we analyze a correlation matrix as if it were a covariance matrix, some parameter estimates may still be the correct standardized estimates but the SEs are usually incorrect.

So, perhaps you can cite papers on analyzing correlation matrices in SEM, e.g.,

Cudeck, R. (1989). Analysis of correlation matrices using covariance structure models. Psychological Bulletin, 105(2), 317–327. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.105.2.317

P.S.: There are ways to analyze correlations correctly in SEM but this is another topic.

-- Shu Fai

However, the variance of y is not a free parameter in the model, but a function of the estimates of b, the variance of x, and the variance of the error term of y (displayed as "y ~~ y" in the parameter estimate table).

So, the sampling variance of beta, the standardized regression coefficient, is a function of the sampling variance and covariance of the estimates of b, the variance of x, and the variance of the error term. Even if x is treated as fixed and so it is not an estimate, the estimate of the variance of the error term is not fixed.

Moreover, there are cases in which we would like to treat x variables as random (setting fixed.x = FALSE). In these cases, then sampling variance of estimate of the variance of x (and its covariance with other estimates involved), will affect the SE of the standardized regression coefficient:

# Original data
fit1b <- sem(mod, dat, fixed.x = FALSE)
# Standardized coefficient: Raw data, fixed.x = FALSE
print(standardizedSolution(fit1b)[1, ], nd = 5)
#>   lhs op rhs est.std     se        z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
#> 1   y  ~   x 0.68408 0.0532 12.85804      0  0.57981  0.78836

The following example illustrate how to compute the standardized coefficient using ":=", and the SE, p-value, and CI are identical to those from standardizedSolution() (fixed.x = FALSE):

mod3 <-
"
y ~ b * x
y ~~ evar * y
x ~~ xvar * x
ysd := sqrt((b^2) * xvar + evar)
xsd := sqrt(xvar)
# Self-computed standardized
bstd := b * xsd / ysd
"

library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-12
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.

# Original data
fit3 <- sem(mod3, dat)
print(parameterEstimates(fit3), nd = 5)
#>    lhs op                   rhs label      est      se        z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
#> 1    y  ~                     x     b  0.54183 0.05777  9.37869      0  0.42860  0.65507
#> 2    y ~~                     y  evar  9.81441 1.38797  7.07107      0  7.09404 12.53478
#> 3    x ~~                     x  xvar 29.40457 4.15843  7.07107      0 21.25419 37.55495
#> 4  ysd := sqrt((b^2)*xvar+evar)   ysd  4.29501 0.30370 14.14214      0  3.69977  4.89026
#> 5  xsd :=            sqrt(xvar)   xsd  5.42260 0.38344 14.14214      0  4.67108  6.17412
#> 6 bstd :=             b*xsd/ysd  bstd  0.68408 0.05320 12.85804      0  0.57981  0.78836

In short, we should use standardizedSolution() because it takes into account the sampling variability of the standardizers (the SDs). If we standardize the variables first, their sampling variability, if any, is ignored.

I hope I understood how lavaan works on this regard. Please correct me if I am wrong.

A side issue: For both standardizedSolution() and parameters defined by ":=", standard errors are derived by the delta method:

https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/i4OF4O0_Uv8/m/ZvkjkTPuAAAJ

Actually, in the one-IV-one-DV simple regression model above, you may recall the beta is equal to the Pearson's r between x and y. We know that the sampling distribution of Pearson's r is asymmetric (unless the population correlation is zero) and so usually we form asymmetric CI fora Pearson's r using methods such as Fisher's z transformation.

cor.test(dat$x, dat$y)
#> 95 percent confidence interval:
#>  0.5633636 0.7762064
#> sample estimates:
#>       cor
#> 0.6840844

Delta method yields symmetric CI. Nevertheless, in this example, the Fisher's z CI, [.536, .776] and delta method CI, [.580, .788], are not too different except for the lower limit.
